question_text: A mobile operator lowers the monthly price of its data bundle and observes that the total quantity of bundles subscribers buy rises. Which principle does this most directly illustrate?
options: The law of supply, where quantity supplied rises as price falls in the short run
The law of demand, where quantity demanded rises as price falls, other things equal
A rightward shift of the demand curve caused by the price reduction
An increase in demand elasticity that automatically raises total revenue
correct_answer: The law of demand, where quantity demanded rises as price falls, other things equal

question_text: An analyst notes that the quantity of broadband demanded changed solely because the price of broadband itself changed, with incomes and tastes unchanged. This is best described as:
options: A rightward shift of the entire demand curve
A movement along the existing demand curve
A leftward shift of the entire demand curve
A change in the position of the supply curve
correct_answer: A movement along the existing demand curve

question_text: When the price of fresh yoghurt rises sharply, many buyers switch to alternatives such as Fanyogo or Fanice instead. In demand analysis these alternatives are best classified as:
options: Complementary goods
Substitute goods
Inferior goods
Giffen goods
correct_answer: Substitute goods

question_text: Among the many determinants of the quantity demanded of a good, economic theory identifies one variable as central to the basic demand relationship. That variable is the:
options: Number of sellers operating in the market
Cost of the inputs used in production
Level of technology available to producers
Price of the good itself
correct_answer: Price of the good itself

question_text: At higher prices a telecom equipment vendor finds it profitable to offer more units, while at lower prices it offers fewer. This relationship between price and quantity offered is captured by the:
options: Law of demand
Law of supply
Law of diminishing marginal utility
Principle of tax incidence
correct_answer: Law of supply

question_text: The market supply curve is drawn holding input costs constant. If the price of a key input such as sugar falls for ice-cream makers, the most likely result is that the supply curve:
options: Shifts to the left, as producers supply less at each price
Becomes perfectly vertical at the equilibrium quantity
Stays fixed while only quantity demanded increases
Shifts to the right, as producers supply more at each price
correct_answer: Shifts to the right, as producers supply more at each price

question_text: Demand for a particular good is described as elastic. This means that:
options: Quantity demanded responds substantially to a change in the good's price
Quantity demanded barely responds to a change in the good's price
Quantity supplied responds substantially to a change in the good's price
Price remains fixed regardless of changes in quantity demanded
correct_answer: Quantity demanded responds substantially to a change in the good's price

question_text: A regulator studies a service that consumers treat as a necessity with few substitutes, so a price increase changes the quantity bought only slightly. Demand for this service is best described as:
options: Elastic
Inelastic
Perfectly elastic
Unit elastic
correct_answer: Inelastic

question_text: On a standard supply-and-demand diagram, the single point at which the supply curve and the demand curve intersect determines the:
options: Price ceiling and the resulting shortage
Price floor and the resulting surplus
Tax incidence borne by buyers and sellers
Equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity
correct_answer: Equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity

question_text: To keep a service affordable, a government sets a maximum legal price below the market equilibrium price. Standard analysis predicts this price ceiling will most likely create:
options: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A new stable equilibrium exactly at the controlled price
An increase in supply that quickly eliminates excess demand
correct_answer: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied

question_text: A government sets a minimum legal price above the market equilibrium to protect suppliers. The most likely consequence of this price floor is:
options: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
An immediate return of the market to its equilibrium
A reduction in quantity supplied below the quantity demanded
A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
correct_answer: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded

question_text: In public finance, the term tax incidence refers specifically to:
options: The statutory rate at which a tax is officially levied
The total revenue a government collects from a tax
How the burden of a tax is distributed among the participants in a market
The administrative cost of collecting and enforcing a tax
correct_answer: How the burden of a tax is distributed among the participants in a market

question_text: When a per-unit tax is imposed on the sellers of a good, the standard model represents its initial effect as:
options: A rightward shift of the supply curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
A leftward (upward) shift of the supply curve
A rotation that makes the demand curve more elastic
correct_answer: A leftward (upward) shift of the supply curve

question_text: Two markets face an identical per-unit tax. In Market A demand is highly inelastic; in Market B demand is highly elastic. Compared with sellers, buyers will tend to bear the larger share of the tax in:
options: Market B, where demand is elastic
Market A, where demand is inelastic
Both markets equally, regardless of elasticity
Neither market, because sellers always remit the tax
correct_answer: Market A, where demand is inelastic

question_text: An economic system in which production and allocation follow long-standing customary patterns and local leaders have the ultimate say is best described as a:
options: Command economy
Market economy
Traditional economy
Mixed economy
correct_answer: Traditional economy

question_text: Twentieth-century experience suggests that a command economy tends to fail largely because:
options: Prices adjust too quickly for producers to keep pace with demand
Private firms refuse to compete once the state withdraws
A central authority cannot efficiently gather and act on the information needed to allocate resources
Consumers are given too many choices to coordinate production
correct_answer: A central authority cannot efficiently gather and act on the information needed to allocate resources

question_text: A mixed economy is best characterised as one in which:
options: A central planner sets all prices, wages and output levels
Custom and tradition determine nearly all economic decisions
Market forces operate with no government involvement of any kind
Markets allocate most resources while governments intervene to correct market failures
correct_answer: Markets allocate most resources while governments intervene to correct market failures

question_text: Advocates argue that a market economy can be self-optimising because, when individuals are free to pursue their own interests, the system tends to:
options: Eliminate the need for any property rights or contracts
Guarantee an equal distribution of income across society
Prevent monopolies from ever arising in any industry
Settle at a stable equilibrium of supply, consumption and prices
correct_answer: Settle at a stable equilibrium of supply, consumption and prices

question_text: In a perfectly competitive market each individual buyer and seller is assumed to be a price taker. This assumption follows from the fact that:
options: A single dominant firm sets the price that all others follow
The government fixes the price at which all trades must occur
There are so many participants that no single one can influence the market price
Buyers and sellers collude to maintain a common price
correct_answer: There are so many participants that no single one can influence the market price

question_text: Compared with a competitive industry, a profit-maximising monopoly is generally expected to:
options: Produce more output and charge a lower price
Produce less output and charge a higher price
Produce the same output but at a lower cost
Charge a lower price while expanding total output
correct_answer: Produce less output and charge a higher price

question_text: An industry is termed a natural monopoly when:
options: Two firms can always supply the market more cheaply than one
The government legally bans all but one firm from entering
Firms naturally collude to behave as though they were one
A single firm can supply the whole market at lower cost than two or more firms could
correct_answer: A single firm can supply the whole market at lower cost than two or more firms could

question_text: Where a genuine natural monopoly exists, a government wishing to avoid wasteful duplication of infrastructure may reasonably choose to:
options: Tolerate the single firm but subject it to regulation
Force several firms to compete regardless of cost
Withdraw entirely and leave the market unregulated
Nationalise every competing firm in the wider economy
correct_answer: Tolerate the single firm but subject it to regulation

question_text: Within the logic of a market economy, the primary justification for governments intervening through regulators and other institutions is that:
options: Markets can fail, and intervention may correct such failures
Markets always allocate resources perfectly without help
Government planning is inherently superior to all markets
Competition should be eliminated to simplify oversight
correct_answer: Markets can fail, and intervention may correct such failures

question_text: An economist distinguishes a change in demand from a change in quantity demanded. A change in demand (a shift of the curve) is caused by:
options: A change in the good's own price alone
Movement to a different point on the same demand curve
A change in a determinant other than the good's own price, such as income or tastes
A simultaneous and exactly offsetting change in supply
correct_answer: A change in a determinant other than the good's own price, such as income or tastes

question_text: One reason a monopoly is considered socially harmful is that its output is typically produced:
options: More efficiently and at a lower cost than under competition
Less efficiently and at a higher cost than under competition
At exactly the competitive level of cost and efficiency
Only when it is directly subsidised by the government
correct_answer: Less efficiently and at a higher cost than under competition

question_text: Before the 1980s, telecommunications services in most countries were typically provided by:
options: Numerous competing private operators
Independent regional cooperatives
State-owned monopolies
Foreign-owned multinational consortia
correct_answer: State-owned monopolies

question_text: A factor underpinning the pre-1980s telecom monopoly paradigm was economic: high network build costs and low demand meant a second operator could not easily recover its costs. This gave the industry the character of a:
options: Natural monopoly
Perfectly contestable market
Fully deregulated free market
Command-economy consumer good
correct_answer: Natural monopoly

question_text: A political factor behind early state telecom monopolies was that governments:
options: Were barred by treaty from licensing any private firm
Lacked any ministry capable of running a postal service
Preferred to auction spectrum to the highest private bidder
Wished to retain state control over communications, often treating them as an extension of postal networks
correct_answer: Wished to retain state control over communications, often treating them as an extension of postal networks

question_text: In telecommunications, liberalization is best defined as:
options: The transfer of an operator's ownership from the state to private hands
The intervention of government to achieve specific market outcomes
The process of transition from a monopoly market to a competitive one
The setting of technical standards common to all operators
correct_answer: The process of transition from a monopoly market to a competitive one

question_text: A central element of liberalization is the removal of exclusivities from the former monopoly fixed-network operator, commonly called the incumbent. The direct effect of removing these exclusivities is to:
options: Allow new entrants to compete in services that were previously monopolised
Transfer the incumbent's shares to private investors
Guarantee the incumbent a permanently protected market
Impose price caps on every service the incumbent offers
correct_answer: Allow new entrants to compete in services that were previously monopolised

question_text: Privatization in the telecom sector refers to:
options: The transition of a market from monopoly to competition
The imposition of universal-service obligations on operators
The transfer of ownership of an operator from the state to the private sector
The creation of an independent national regulatory authority
correct_answer: The transfer of ownership of an operator from the state to the private sector

question_text: Governments have privatized incumbent operators in different ways. Selling a stake to a single strategic investor, rather than via a broad public share sale, has been the more common approach in:
options: Highly industrialised countries
Countries that have no incumbent operator
Countries that retained a full state monopoly
Developing countries
correct_answer: Developing countries

question_text: A country opens its mobile market to several competing firms but keeps the incumbent fixed-line operator fully state-owned. This situation is best described as:
options: Privatization without liberalization
Liberalization without privatization of the incumbent
Both full liberalization and full privatization
Neither liberalization nor privatization
correct_answer: Liberalization without privatization of the incumbent

question_text: In the context of the telecom sector, regulation is best defined as:
options: Government intervention in markets to achieve certain desired outcomes
The complete removal of government from market activity
The transfer of state assets into private ownership
The voluntary self-policing of firms with no oversight
correct_answer: Government intervention in markets to achieve certain desired outcomes

question_text: Regulation is sometimes said to take three basic forms. The form that establishes a common, legally enforceable platform for all businesses, such as rules governing electrical supply or company accounting, is:
options: Competition regulation
Public policy regulation
Technical standardization
Voluntary self-regulation
correct_answer: Technical standardization

question_text: Legislation that controls the supply of goods such as alcohol, gambling or pornography because doing so is believed to serve the public interest is an example of:
options: Technical standardization
Competition regulation
Public policy regulation
Co-regulation
correct_answer: Public policy regulation

question_text: The form of regulation that seeks to create and maintain fair competitive relationships between businesses, and between businesses and consumers, is:
options: Technical standardization
Competition regulation
Public policy regulation
Zero regulation
correct_answer: Competition regulation

question_text: Although telecom regulation can take all three basic forms, the principal focus of contemporary regulation of the telecommunications services industry is:
options: The standardisation of accounting rules across all industries
The control of socially sensitive goods such as gambling
The creation, nourishment and maintenance of competitive markets
The elimination of private ownership from the sector
correct_answer: The creation, nourishment and maintenance of competitive markets

question_text: Among the widely accepted regulatory objectives in the telecom sector is the aim to:
options: Guarantee a fixed profit margin to every licensed operator
Restrict connectivity to commercially attractive urban areas
Promote universal access to basic telecommunications services
Prevent any new operators from entering the market
correct_answer: Promote universal access to basic telecommunications services

question_text: A recognised regulatory objective is that, where competitive markets do not exist or have failed, the regulator should:
options: Guarantee the dominant firm protection from all competitors
Prevent abuses of market power such as excessive pricing by dominant firms
Withdraw oversight so the market can correct itself
Fix every operator's retail prices at identical levels
correct_answer: Prevent abuses of market power such as excessive pricing by dominant firms

question_text: Which statement best captures the distinction between policy and law as drawn in the course material?
options: Law can compel or prohibit behaviour, whereas policy merely guides actions toward a desired outcome
Policy can compel behaviour, whereas law only offers guidance
Policy and law are identical and fully interchangeable terms
Regulation sets broad goals while policy enforces them in court
correct_answer: Law can compel or prohibit behaviour, whereas policy merely guides actions toward a desired outcome

question_text: In the policy-to-practice chain, regulation is primarily concerned with:
options: Translating the objectives of policy decisions into practical rules and decisions
Setting the broad long-term vision before any policy exists
Replacing the need for any underlying legislation
Auditing the personal finances of government ministers
correct_answer: Translating the objectives of policy decisions into practical rules and decisions

question_text: In many countries before reform, a single ministry or government unit often acted simultaneously as:
options: An independent regulator fully separated from the operator
A purely commercial firm with no policy responsibilities
Policy maker, policy implementer and operator of the telephone service
A neutral standards body with no operational role
correct_answer: Policy maker, policy implementer and operator of the telephone service

question_text: The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) is best described as:
options: A private consortium of the world's largest mobile operators
A regional trade bloc that sets tariffs on telecom equipment
A specialised agency of the United Nations responsible for information and communication technology issues
A commercial standards firm owned by equipment vendors
correct_answer: A specialised agency of the United Nations responsible for information and communication technology issues

question_text: Within the ITU's three-sector structure, the sector that manages the international radio-frequency spectrum and satellite-orbit resources is:
options: ITU-R (Radiocommunication)
ITU-T (Standardization)
ITU-D (Development)
ITU-P (Policy)
correct_answer: ITU-R (Radiocommunication)

question_text: The ITU sector responsible for standardizing global telecommunications, except for radio matters, is:
options: ITU-R (Radiocommunication)
ITU-D (Development)
ITU-T (Standardization)
ITU-S (Spectrum)
correct_answer: ITU-T (Standardization)

question_text: Helping to spread equitable, sustainable and affordable access to ICTs is the principal role of which ITU sector?
options: ITU-R (Radiocommunication)
ITU-D (Development)
ITU-T (Standardization)
ITU-A (Access)
correct_answer: ITU-D (Development)

question_text: The World Trade Organization's Agreement on Basic Telecommunications (the BTA) primarily:
options: Allocates radio spectrum directly to individual operators
Establishes rules for competition and promotes open investment in telecoms across countries
Sets the retail tariffs that operators may charge consumers
Issues operating licences to individual carriers in member states
correct_answer: Establishes rules for competition and promotes open investment in telecoms across countries

question_text: One of the six basic principles of the WTO Reference Paper on Regulation is that:
options: The dominant operator should also serve as the regulator
Licensing criteria should be kept confidential from competitors
Scarce resources should be reserved for the incumbent operator
There should be a regulatory body independent of operating companies
correct_answer: There should be a regulatory body independent of operating companies

question_text: The WTO Reference Paper requires telecom regulators to be independent of operating companies. On independence from government, the material indicates that regulators are:
options: Not necessarily independent of governments, though greater independence is often regarded as better
Required to be wholly controlled by the relevant ministry
Required to be completely independent of government in every respect
Required to be jointly owned by the operators they regulate
correct_answer: Not necessarily independent of governments, though greater independence is often regarded as better

question_text: According to the framework for regulation, the laws passed by governments to enable regulation typically:
options: Guarantee monopoly status to the incumbent operator
Appoint regulatory bodies and confer on them powers to take action
Remove all accountability requirements from regulators
Fix the retail prices of every regulated service
correct_answer: Appoint regulatory bodies and confer on them powers to take action

question_text: Which option best lists the categories of law that bear specifically on the telecommunications services industry?
options: Sector-specific telecom law, competition and fair-trading law, and other relevant law such as privacy
Criminal law, maritime law and constitutional law only
Tax law, employment law and intellectual-property law only
Banking law, insurance law and environmental law only
correct_answer: Sector-specific telecom law, competition and fair-trading law, and other relevant law such as privacy

question_text: Provisions enacted by bodies such as ECOWAS or the WTO take force in a member or signatory country when they are:
options: Transposed into national law in accordance with treaty obligations
Published on the regional body's website
Approved by a majority of the country's operators
Adopted automatically without any national action
correct_answer: Transposed into national law in accordance with treaty obligations

question_text: The framework notes that the function of regulation may be split between two or more bodies. A risk a country must manage when doing so is that:
options: Poorly designed division of functions can lead to disagreements and slow decision-making
A single regulator will inevitably capture the entire market
Operators will be unable to obtain any licence at all
Spectrum will automatically be allocated free of charge
correct_answer: Poorly designed division of functions can lead to disagreements and slow decision-making

question_text: Listed in increasing order of intrusiveness, the styles of regulation are:
options: Formal regulation, co-regulation, self-regulation, zero regulation
Zero regulation, self-regulation, co-regulation, formal regulation
Self-regulation, zero regulation, formal regulation, co-regulation
Co-regulation, formal regulation, zero regulation, self-regulation
correct_answer: Zero regulation, self-regulation, co-regulation, formal regulation

question_text: An industry described as operating under zero regulation is one in which:
options: A regulator intervenes minutely in daily operations
Firms jointly agree binding rules under a watchdog
Prices are set directly by a government ministry
Market forces are allowed to work with no external intervention
correct_answer: Market forces are allowed to work with no external intervention

question_text: Self-regulation, in which the players in an industry regulate themselves, tends to be MOST effective when:
options: There is a high convergence of interest among the stakeholders
There are strong commercial conflicts between the players
A single firm dominates and distrusts all the others
The regulator intervenes in every operational decision
correct_answer: There is a high convergence of interest among the stakeholders

question_text: A frequently cited benefit of self-regulation is that:
options: Companies usually understand their own businesses better than an external regulator does
It removes all costs of regulation from consumers and industry
It guarantees that no company will ever act opportunistically
It eliminates the need for any underlying legislation
correct_answer: Companies usually understand their own businesses better than an external regulator does

question_text: Co-regulation is best described as an arrangement in which:
options: Firms operate with no oversight of any kind
The regulator dictates every technical and pricing decision
The regulator joins industry players in a joint forum rather than regulating purely from outside
A foreign body assumes all regulatory authority
correct_answer: The regulator joins industry players in a joint forum rather than regulating purely from outside

question_text: While potentially very successful, co-regulation is particularly vulnerable to:
options: An immediate and total loss of all regulatory powers
The automatic capture of the regulator by consumers
Role ambiguity and differing perceptions of what each player will do
A legal prohibition on any form of industry collaboration
correct_answer: Role ambiguity and differing perceptions of what each player will do

question_text: Regulation is described as intrusive when the regulator:
options: Lays down only general principles and leaves methods to firms
Withdraws entirely and lets market forces operate
Intervenes often and minutely in the day-to-day running of a company's business
Limits itself to publishing non-binding guidelines
correct_answer: Intervenes often and minutely in the day-to-day running of a company's business

question_text: One reason intrusive regulation is considered undesirable is that:
options: It always reduces the total cost of administering regulation
It guarantees that competitive market forces will prevail
The regulator effectively becomes a proxy manager of the industry, weakening operators' freedom
It removes the regulator's responsibility for outcomes
correct_answer: The regulator effectively becomes a proxy manager of the industry, weakening operators' freedom

question_text: A good regulator is advised to make regulation pervasive rather than intrusive. This means regulation should:
options: Influence operators broadly while letting them manage their own affairs within the spirit of the rules
Dictate the precise technical solution for every operator
Have as little impact as possible on companies in the market
Apply to only a single dominant operator at a time
correct_answer: Influence operators broadly while letting them manage their own affairs within the spirit of the rules

question_text: The main instruments through which regulation is accomplished include authorizations, rules, determinations, consents and:
options: Guidelines
Share buy-backs
Spectrum auctions
Corporate tax assessments
correct_answer: Guidelines

question_text: A system of authorization may issue specific authorizations and general authorizations. These correspond respectively to:
options: Spectrum licences and numbering plans
Individual operator licences and class licences
Price caps and interconnection orders
Consents and determinations
correct_answer: Individual operator licences and class licences

question_text: Determinations are instruments of ongoing regulation that, in effect:
options: Permanently revoke an operator's licence without appeal
Replace the underlying legislation entirely
Elaborate the rules, for example in the periodic review of price controls
Carry no legal force and are merely advisory
correct_answer: Elaborate the rules, for example in the periodic review of price controls

question_text: A consent is best understood as:
options: An order that imposes an additional obligation on an operator
An informal guideline that carries no legal status
A penalty levied for breach of a licence condition
A negative determination that formally relieves an operator from complying with a requirement
correct_answer: A negative determination that formally relieves an operator from complying with a requirement

question_text: Guidelines differ from rules and determinations in that guidelines:
options: Have greater legal force than the licence conditions themselves
Do not in themselves possess legal status and are usually written in user-friendly language
Can be issued only by the courts after a successful appeal
Automatically revoke a licence the moment they are breached
correct_answer: Do not in themselves possess legal status and are usually written in user-friendly language

question_text: A key reason regulators consult widely before finalising instruments is that consultation:
options: Transfers formal decision-making power to the consulted parties
Removes the regulator's obligation to justify its decisions
Gives industry ownership and pre-knowledge of decisions and enriches decision-making
Guarantees that no party will ever appeal the outcome
correct_answer: Gives industry ownership and pre-knowledge of decisions and enriches decision-making

question_text: An appeal against a regulator's action may be brought on the grounds of law (illegality), procedure (misadministration) or:
options: Profitability (commercial loss)
Logic (irrationality)
Popularity (public disapproval)
Convenience (administrative delay)
correct_answer: Logic (irrationality)

question_text: Which of the following is a recognised enforcement power available to a regulator dealing with rule breaches?
options: Seizing ownership of a competitor's shares
Setting the personal salaries of company directors
Revoking a licence, or imposing fines and compliance orders
Banning the company's customers from switching providers
correct_answer: Revoking a licence, or imposing fines and compliance orders

question_text: Regarding the funding of national regulatory authorities, the typical arrangement is that:
options: Operators are legally barred from contributing any funds
Regulators are funded solely by fines collected from consumers
Funding comes entirely from international donor agencies
Governments assume primary responsibility but usually pass the cost onto industry through fees
correct_answer: Governments assume primary responsibility but usually pass the cost onto industry through fees

question_text: The concept of regulatory hazard refers to the fact that:
options: Regulators are physically endangered when inspecting networks
Regulation always removes all risk from the telecom market
Operators face no consequences for breaching the rules
Regulatory power, if exercised unwisely, can distort markets and damage the industry it serves
correct_answer: Regulatory power, if exercised unwisely, can distort markets and damage the industry it serves

question_text: Regulatory capture occurs when:
options: The regulator becomes paralysed and issues no decisions at all
Operators are captured and run directly by the regulator
Consumers take over the day-to-day running of the regulator
The regulator identifies too closely with, and so serves the interests of, the industry it regulates
correct_answer: The regulator identifies too closely with, and so serves the interests of, the industry it regulates

question_text: The information asymmetry, or knowledge gap, that regulators face arises because:
options: Regulators are legally forbidden from collecting any data
Consumers deliberately conceal their preferences from the regulator
Operators are required to share none of their financial records
The companies being regulated usually know far more about the business than the regulator does
correct_answer: The companies being regulated usually know far more about the business than the regulator does

question_text: Regulators issue licences to companies primarily to authorise them to:
options: Operate telecommunications networks and provide telecommunications services
Manufacture and export telecommunications equipment
Set the national monetary policy for the sector
Audit the financial accounts of rival operators
correct_answer: Operate telecommunications networks and provide telecommunications services

question_text: Beyond granting permission to operate, a telecommunications licence characteristically specifies:
options: The retail prices that every other operator must charge
The internal staffing structure of the regulator itself
What facilities a company may deploy, what services it may offer, and how it must interact with other businesses
The personal tax obligations of the company's directors
correct_answer: What facilities a company may deploy, what services it may offer, and how it must interact with other businesses

question_text: In addition to facilities and services, major licences may govern access to scarce resources such as spectrum and numbers, and commonly require companies to pay:
options: Upfront fees when the licence is awarded and annual payments thereafter
A fixed share of profits to every competing operator
Nothing, since licences are always granted free of charge
A one-time deposit that is fully refunded on expiry
correct_answer: Upfront fees when the licence is awarded and annual payments thereafter

question_text: Historically, telecom licences were allocated separately for different sub-markets, for example fixed networks, mobile networks or paging. The main characteristic of this approach was that licences:
options: Were technology- and service-neutral by design
Imposed identical terms across every market segment
Differentiated between specific technologies and services
Were never tied to any particular type of service
correct_answer: Differentiated between specific technologies and services

question_text: Recent technological convergence, which lets different platforms deliver a wider range of services, has prompted some regulators to move toward:
options: Stricter technology-specific licensing for each platform
Technology- and service-neutral licensing
The complete abolition of all forms of licensing
Permanent exclusive licences for incumbent operators
correct_answer: Technology- and service-neutral licensing

question_text: A technology-neutral licence to provide a telephone service is one that:
options: Requires the company to use a specified fixed-line technology
Forbids the company from offering any voice service at all
Mandates a single government-approved equipment vendor
Lets the company choose whether to use a fixed network or a particular wireless technology
correct_answer: Lets the company choose whether to use a fixed network or a particular wireless technology

question_text: The two main types of licence awarded to telecom companies are:
options: Spectrum licences and numbering licences
Import licences and export licences
Provisional licences and probationary licences
Individual operator licences and class licences (general authorizations)
correct_answer: Individual operator licences and class licences (general authorizations)

question_text: Individual operator licences are used primarily where:
options: The market segment has unlimited room for new entrants
No scarce resources of any kind are involved
Identical terms are wanted for every business in the segment
The number of licences is limited, dominance is likely, or specific resources such as spectrum must be allocated
correct_answer: The number of licences is limited, dominance is likely, or specific resources such as spectrum must be allocated

question_text: Class licences (general authorizations) are characterised by the fact that they:
options: Are tailored individually to one named operator
Set out identical terms of operation for all businesses in a market segment, such as ISPs
Are reserved exclusively for the incumbent operator
Apply only where radio spectrum must be allocated
correct_answer: Set out identical terms of operation for all businesses in a market segment, such as ISPs

question_text: A current trend favours replacing individual operator licences with general authorizations wherever possible because doing so:
options: Simplifies regulation, helps ensure a level playing field, and is more flexible to market change
Maximises the upfront revenue collected from each operator
Guarantees the incumbent a protected monopoly position
Eliminates the need for any regulator in the sector
correct_answer: Simplifies regulation, helps ensure a level playing field, and is more flexible to market change

question_text: One licensing objective treats basic telecommunications as an essential public service. This justifies:
options: Removing all oversight once the market is privatised
Retaining some controls to ensure services are provided in the public interest
Reserving service provision for a single state monopoly forever
Allowing operators to serve only the most profitable customers
correct_answer: Retaining some controls to ensure services are provided in the public interest

question_text: Network roll-out and service-coverage obligations are often written into licences to advance which licensing objective?
options: Generation of one-time government auction revenue
Protection of the incumbent from any competition
Standardisation of company accounting practices
Expansion of networks and services, and universal service
correct_answer: Expansion of networks and services, and universal service

question_text: When a state-owned incumbent is privatized, a licence is necessary because it:
options: Transfers ownership of the regulator to the investor
Specifies what the investor is buying and what the government expects from the operator
Guarantees the investor permanent freedom from regulation
Removes the operator's obligation to serve any customers
correct_answer: Specifies what the investor is buying and what the government expects from the operator

question_text: Licensing can be used to regulate market structure, most directly by:
options: Fixing the wholesale price of every network input
Determining the number of operators licensed to provide services
Setting the wages paid to operators' employees
Selecting the equipment vendors operators must use
correct_answer: Determining the number of operators licensed to provide services

question_text: Licence conditions intended to create a level playing field and limit incumbents' abuse of dominance are generally referred to as:
options: Universal-service obligations
Spectrum-refarming provisions
Tariff-rebalancing schedules
Anti-competitive safeguards or fair-trading conditions
correct_answer: Anti-competitive safeguards or fair-trading conditions

question_text: Finite resources such as radio spectrum, numbers and rights of way should, as a licensing objective, be allocated:
options: Entirely to the operator with the longest history
On a first-come basis with no regard to efficiency
Only to operators owned by the national government
Between operators fairly, efficiently and in the public interest
correct_answer: Between operators fairly, efficiently and in the public interest

question_text: Licensing can generate government revenue in two characteristic ways:
options: One-time revenues from auctions and continuing revenue from annual licence fees
Confiscation of operator profits and seizure of their assets
Personal income taxes levied on the regulator's own staff
Mandatory donations collected from international agencies
correct_answer: One-time revenues from auctions and continuing revenue from annual licence fees

question_text: Consumer-protection conditions in telecom licences commonly address matters such as:
options: Billing practices, complaint mechanisms and mandatory services like emergency calls
The internal share structure of the operator
The personal credit ratings of company directors
The choice of the regulator's external auditors
correct_answer: Billing practices, complaint mechanisms and mandatory services like emergency calls

question_text: By clearly defining the rights and obligations of the operator and the regulator, a licence advances the objective of:
options: Regulatory certainty, which builds confidence and helps attract investment
Spectrum refarming across competing operators
Eliminating the regulator's discretion entirely
Guaranteeing every operator an equal market share
correct_answer: Regulatory certainty, which builds confidence and helps attract investment

question_text: Radio spectrum is a scarce resource whose international allocation is governed by rules intended to maximise its use while minimising cross-border interference. These rules are managed by the:
options: International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
World Trade Organization (WTO)
Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
Individual operators within each country
correct_answer: International Telecommunication Union (ITU)

question_text: Although telephone numbers are in principle infinite, they are treated as a scarce resource partly because:
options: There are physically only a few thousand digits in existence
Each number requires its own dedicated radio frequency
A given number can be used by only one country worldwide
People can hold only a limited number of digits in short-term memory, and numbers must be allocated in meaningful blocks
correct_answer: People can hold only a limited number of digits in short-term memory, and numbers must be allocated in meaningful blocks

question_text: Number portability is a mechanism by which:
options: The operator permanently owns every number it issues
The subscriber, rather than the operator, owns the number and can take it when switching providers
Numbers are auctioned to the highest-bidding operator
Subscribers must change numbers each time they switch providers
correct_answer: The subscriber, rather than the operator, owns the number and can take it when switching providers

question_text: In allocating spectrum, a regulator may auction it to the highest bidder or allocate it at low cost. Allocating spectrum at low cost is typically intended to:
options: Reduce prices or encourage the rollout of new services
Maximise the one-time revenue collected by the government
Guarantee that only one operator can ever use the band
Remove the need to manage interference between users
correct_answer: Reduce prices or encourage the rollout of new services

question_text: A primary reason spectrum must be allocated through agreements such as licences, rather than used freely, is to:
options: Increase the number of digits available for telephone numbers
Allow every operator to broadcast on any frequency it wishes
Remove the need for any international coordination of frequencies
Ensure it is properly distributed and that users do not interfere with one another
correct_answer: Ensure it is properly distributed and that users do not interfere with one another

question_text: The core principle of interconnection is that:
options: Each operator should keep its subscribers isolated from rivals' networks
Only operators of an equal size are required to interconnect
Interconnection is required only between international carriers
Everyone should be able to communicate with everyone else, regardless of which network they subscribe to
correct_answer: Everyone should be able to communicate with everyone else, regardless of which network they subscribe to
